summary: Defines two new categories of IP performance metrics: spatial metrics, which measure the performance of parts of a path, and multicast metrics, covering multiple measurement points. They extend the earlier two-point approach.

plainLanguage.summary: Rather than timing the whole trip, you time each leg of it, and for group broadcasts you time each listener.

questions: how is multicast group delay measured
what is a routers digest in ippm
subtitle: IPPM metrics that look inside a path, segment by segment, and across a whole multicast group.

tldr.problem: The existing IP Performance Metrics measure only end-to-end performance between two points. They cannot say which part of a path is at fault or how a group of receivers is served.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines seven spatial metrics (vectors and segment samples that observe one packet at several routers) and three one-to-group vector metrics, plus group statistics such as mean delay, loss ratio and delay variation ranges across receivers.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a standard vocabulary for per-segment and per-receiver measurement, with reporting guidance and a design choice that keeps data volume manageable. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6248.

today: RFC 5644 is a Proposed Standard from October 2009 and is updated by RFC 6248. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Extend the IPPM Metrics
sections.content:
The IETF had standardized IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) for measuring end-to-end performance between two points. RFC 5644 defines two new categories that cover multiple measurement points: spatial metrics for segments of a source-to-destination path, and one-to-group metrics for a source and many destinations, such as a multicast tree. All of them are derived from one-way end-to-end metrics and follow the IPPM framework of RFC 2330.

The RFC lists what each category is for. Spatial metrics help decompose an inter-domain path to see each AS's share of the end-to-end performance, support traffic engineering and troubleshooting by showing where delay accumulates or packets are lost, and let segment measurements be reused to reach large-scale coverage. One-to-group metrics help design and engineer multicast trees and MPLS point-to-multipoint LSPs, evaluate multicast service quality, and describe performance requirements for multiparty communication.

The scope is limited to a single source packet or stream, and to active measurement, meaning packets dedicated to testing. Passive measurement of user traffic is out of scope. Group-to-one and group-to-group topologies are also out of scope, although the RFC sketches how they could be organized from one-to-group measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: Old measurements only told you how long the whole trip took. These new ones tell you which part was slow, and how each person in a group was treated.

sections.title: Points of Interest, Vectors and Matrices
sections.content:
A point of interest is a host that collects measurements. For spatial metrics these are a (possibly arbitrary) subset of the routers on the path, called the routers digest. For one-to-group metrics they are the destination hosts. A metric is spatial if a measuring host is neither the source nor a destination of the packet, and one-to-group if one source sends a packet that is potentially received by more than one destination.

A vector is a set of singletons (single atomic results) that all correspond to one source packet seen at different hosts, for example the one-way delays dT1 to dTN at N receivers. Several vectors form a matrix, which shows performance in both space (rows, one per point of interest) and time (columns, one per packet). A one-dimensional matrix corresponds to a sample in simple point-to-point measurement.

A reference point is the server, usually centralized and run by a network operator, where statistical calculations are carried out. It is distinct from the measurement hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: A vector is one note's trip timed at every stop. A matrix is a whole stack of notes, each timed at every stop, laid out like a spreadsheet.

sections.title: Spatial Metrics
sections.content:
Three spatial vector metrics split an end-to-end metric along the path: Type-P-Spatial-One-way-Delay-Vector, Type-P-Spatial-Packet-Loss-Vector and Type-P-Spatial-One-way-ipdv-Vector. For delay, a packet sent at time T yields the values dT1 to dTn at routers H1 to Hn plus the end-to-end dT; a router entry is undefined if the packet does not pass within the loss threshold. For loss, each router gets a Boolean, where 0 means the packet was seen there and 1 means it was not.

Four segment samples then use the vectors to measure between two routers Ha and Hb over time: Type-P-Segment-One-way-Delay-Stream (dTk.b minus dTk.a), Type-P-Segment-Packet-Loss-Stream, Type-P-Segment-ipdv-prev-Stream (delay variation using the previous packet) and Type-P-Segment-One-way-ipdv-min-Stream (delay variation measured against the minimum delay).

The RFC is frank about odd results. Delay values can seem to decrease along the path, for instance from clock synchronization problems, from routers being reordered after reconvergence such as recovery from a link failure, or from where the measurement point sits inside a device. As an example of clock trouble, a 500 km fibre path has a minimum delay of 2.5 ms, but a collection point with 8 ms clock resolution cannot see it. Segment samples are invalid if Ha or Hb leaves the path or their order changes. The ipdv-prev sample is sensitive to the inter-packet interval, which the ingress point of interest does not control, while the ipdv-min sample is less sensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Time a package at every post office along its route. Subtracting the times at two post offices tells you how long it spent between them, and a missing stamp tells you where it got lost.

sections.title: One-to-Group Vectors
sections.content:
Three one-to-group metrics collect the matching end-to-end singletons for one sender and N receivers: Type-P-One-to-group-Delay-Vector, Type-P-One-to-group-Packet-Loss-Vector and Type-P-One-to-group-ipdv-Vector. Each is a set of the corresponding one-way singletons from RFC 2679, RFC 2680 or RFC 3393, one per receiver.

An optional parameter, Gr, identifies the receiving group; it is the multicast group address when the packets are sent over IP multicast. It is optional so that the metric also applies to plain unicast measurement with one receiver. The RFC stresses that applied to a one-to-one topology, the one-to-group metrics give exactly the same results as the corresponding one-to-one metrics. The idea extends the single path to a path tree.
sections.plainLanguage: One teacher sends the same note to a whole class and writes down how long it took to reach each child, and whether it arrived at all.

sections.title: Group Statistics
sections.content:
Raw vectors are hard to read as a group, and delays are not directly comparable because receivers are at different distances. The RFC therefore defines statistics that summarize one-to-one results across all receivers. This covers relative performance, the difference in what users experience, which matters for services such as online gaming where a very small difference in delay might decide the outcome.

Delay: RnMD is the mean delay at receiver n, GMD is the mean of those means across the group, GRMD is the range (max minus min of RnMD), and GMMD is the maximum of RnMD.

Loss: RnLR is the loss ratio at receiver n, GLR is the loss ratio over all losses of all receivers, and GRLR is the range max(RnLR) minus min(RnLR); the RFC recommends reporting both the maximum and minimum, not only the difference. RnCLR is a comparative loss ratio whose denominator is the maximum number of packets received at any receiver rather than the number sent.

Delay variation: GRDV is max(RnDV) minus min(RnDV). RnDV is usually expressed as the 1-10^(-3) quantile of one-way delay minus the minimum one-way delay. For a more demanding service the RFC suggests the 1-10^-5 quantile, and the quantile used should be recorded with the results.

Statistics can be computed over time, over space, or both. These two-level statistics give the same result whichever dimension is computed first. Packet loss complicates the matrix because different receivers lose different packets. The RFC mentions filling a gap with the average of the two adjacent values, or weighting each reported statistic, but treats the details as out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: To compare kids in a class, you take the average time for each kid, then look at the average of everyone and at the gap between the quickest and slowest.

sections.title: Scalability, Reporting and Registration
sections.content:
Measurement multiplies the data: storage grows with both the number of metrics and the number of points of interest. Points of interest can send the whole sample (centralized calculation) or only computed statistics (distributed calculation). Sending statistics saves bandwidth at the reference point, but may hide patterns such as which packets were lost. One suggested approach is to send statistics first and request detailed results only when needed, possibly in off-peak time.

The aggregation order matters for data volume. In Method 1, each point of interest computes statistics over time and reports them, so the volume depends on the computation period and not on the number of test packets. In Method 2, every sample must be reported, so volume grows with the number of test packets, which risks a denial of service toward the reference point and makes dimensioning hard to validate. The RFC defines its metrics on Method 1. It also notes that a one-to-many test sends fewer packets than arrive, since copies reach many destinations, so the test rate must not disturb the network.

Reporting rules build on RFC 2679 and RFC 2680. A spatial vector MUST include the points of interest, ordered along the path (the order MAY be inferred from TTL, Hop Limit or MPLS information), and MUST include the timestamping uncertainty compared to wire-time; for example, internal delays of up to three milliseconds mean a minimum reported uncertainty of 3 ms if the delay is unknown. One-to-group reports SHOULD include the path tree or set of paths, the group size and the measurement method. The RFC also lists an information model of the data elements and registers the metrics in the IANA IPPM Metrics Registry defined by RFC 4148.
sections.plainLanguage: If a thousand helpers all mail every single measurement to one office, the office gets buried. It is better if each helper sends a short summary.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the underlying delay, loss and delay-variation RFCs apply. In addition, someone may spoof a point of interest or a point of interest may itself send corrupt results, in order to steer traffic engineering decisions remotely.

For spatial metrics, packets crafted to match the hash function used to detect packets could cause a DoS attack toward the reference point. Reports reveal per-segment performance and node identities, which an attacker could use to find weak points such as a congested node, so reports should be protected, for example with encrypted sessions or secured networks.

For one-to-group metrics, reports from a huge number of probes may overload the reference point. The RFC suggests considering source authentication protocols from the MSEC group to avoid fraudulent packets, and negotiating the test packet rate before a session. A point of interest could also degrade its own results on purpose to improve the apparent quality of its branch of the multicast tree.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheater could report fake times to trick the network planners, and a pile of reports could swamp the office, so reports must be protected and limited.

items.label: Receiver-n Mean Delay
items.desc: Mean one-way delay at receiver n.

items.label: Group Mean Delay
items.desc: Mean over the group of the RnMD values.

items.label: Receiver-n Loss Ratio
items.desc: Packet loss ratio at receiver n.

items.label: Group Loss Ratio
items.desc: Overall loss ratio over all receivers and packets sent.

items.label: Receiver-n Comparative Loss Ratio
items.desc: Losses at receiver n divided by the most packets received at any receiver.
